courses.subject: AIMS
courses.title: Machine Learning Theory
courses.description:
With machine learning and artificial intelligence now central to many disciplines, it is increasingly important to understand the theoretical tools that make these systems reliable and interpretable in practice. This course focuses on foundational theoretical ideas and analytical derivations that underlie standard machine learning and AI methods. Students will learn to reason about generalization and optimization in machine learning and apply theoretical frameworks to real-world AI workflows through Python-based mini-labs designed to connect theory with practical machine learning.

The course provides an introduction to key theoretical topics in machine learning, including probability and statistics for machine learning (basic concentration inequalities, maximum likelihood, exponential family models), generalization concepts (empirical versus true risk, VC dimension, and capacity norms), kernel methods and feature maps (Mercer’s theorem, representer theorem, and kernel-based learning), optimization theory (gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent, adaptive step-size methods AdaGrad and Adam), online learning and stochastic bandits (regret formulation, upper confidence bound, and Thompson sampling), and the theoretical foundations of generative modeling and diffusion models (score functions and Langevin dynamics).
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence;Pre-requisites: Linear algebra, probability, statistics; Not for students who have taken CSCI5030
courses.course_syllabus:
Week Topic
W1: Probability and Linear Algebra in ML: Basic Definitions and Tools
W2: Statistics in ML: Maximum Likelihood, Exponential Family models
W3: Generalization in ML (Part 1): Empirical vs. Population Risk, Uniform Convergence Analysis
W4: Generalization in ML (Part 2): VC Dimension, Generalization Bounds
W5: Optimization in ML (Part 1): Gradient Descent, Convergence Analysis
W6: Optimization in ML (Part 2): Stochastic Gradient Descent, Adaptive Optimization Methods (AdaGrad/Adam)
W7: Kernel Methods in ML (Part 1): Representer Theorem, Kernel Learning
W8: Kernel Methods in ML (Part 2): Neural Tangent Kernels, Generalization and Optimization in Deep Learning
W9: Online Learning in ML (Part 1): Regret Formulation, Prediction with Expert Advice
W10: Online Learning in ML (Part 2): Exploration–Exploitation Tradeoff, Greedy vs. ε-Greedy Algorithms
W11: Online Learning in ML (Part 3):, UCB Algorithm, Thompson Sampling
W12: Diffusion Models in ML (Part 1): Score function, Score-based Generative Modeling
W13: Diffusion Models in ML (Part 2): Langevin dynamics, Diffusion-based Sampling as Iterative Denoising

courses.required_readings: Lecture Notes to be provided by course instructor.
courses.recommended_readings:
1. Shai Shalev-Shwartz and Shai Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
2. Mehryar Mohri, Afshin Rostamizadeh, and Ameet Talwalkar, *Foundations of Machine Learning*, 2nd Edition, MIT Press, 2018.
3. Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vandenberghe, *Convex Optimization*, Cambridge University Press, 2004.
4. Joe Suzuki, *Kernel Methods for Machine Learning with Math and Python*, Springer Singapore, 2022
5. Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári, *Bandit Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2020.

courses.feedback_evaluation:
Students are encouraged to give comments and make suggestions using the following channels:

1. There are two course evaluations - one before the mid-term, and one at the end of the course. This is a formal channel for students to rate the teacher, the course, and the course tutors. Students can give specific comments or suggestions in addition to the numeric ratings.

2. Students can provide feedbacks using informal channels, such as email, or simply by discussing with the tutors or the instructor directly.
